blocks.text: Study Session 1: Why People Volunteer

A volunteer programme built on a vague hope that people will simply show up out of goodwill tends to struggle. This session introduces a research-based framework for understanding what actually motivates someone to volunteer, and why matching a role to that specific motivation matters as much as the cause itself.
Learning Outcomes

•   Explain the functional approach to volunteer motivation and why it treats motivation as varied rather than uniform. •   Name the six motivational functions volunteering can serve. •   Identify which function or functions likely motivate a specific volunteer. •   Explain why matching a role to a volunteer's actual motivation improves both satisfaction and retention. •   Apply this framework to your own volunteer programme's current or planned roles.
Main Content
Motivation Is Not One Thing

It is tempting to assume everyone who volunteers is motivated by the same basic goodwill, a desire to help. Research on volunteer motivation takes a different, more useful starting point, treating volunteering as behaviour that can serve several distinct psychological functions, and different people performing the identical volunteer activity may be doing so for quite different underlying reasons.

This matters practically because a programme designed around a single assumed motivation, usually the values- based one, altruism and care for the cause, can overlook volunteers who are actually there for other reasons entirely, and miss the chance to design a role and an experience that actually serves what each specific volunteer is looking for.
The Six Motivational Functions

The Values function reflects a volunteer's desire to express humanitarian and altruistic concern for others, the motivation most people assume is universal but which is, in fact, only one of several. The Understanding function reflects a desire to learn new skills or gain knowledge and experience through volunteering. The Social function reflects a desire to strengthen social relationships, spend time with friends, or fit in with a valued group.

The Career function reflects a desire to gain experience or connections that benefit a volunteer's professional future. The Protective function reflects volunteering as a way of reducing negative feelings, such as guilt, or addressing personal difficulties by focusing outward. The Enhancement function reflects a desire for personal growth and self-esteem, volunteering as a way of feeling more capable and valued.
Identifying What Motivates a Specific Volunteer

In practice, identifying a volunteer's likely motivation does not require a formal survey, though one can help for a larger programme. A simple, direct conversation during recruitment, asking what someone hopes to get out of
volunteering, alongside why the cause matters to them, often reveals enough to make a reasonable judgement about which function or functions are most relevant for that specific person.

It is also worth remembering that a single volunteer is often motivated by more than one function simultaneously, a university student might volunteer partly from real values-based concern and partly from a career function, hoping the experience strengthens a future job application. Recognising this mix, rather than forcing a volunteer into one single category, produces a more accurate and useful picture.
Key Practices

Ask directly, during recruitment conversations, what a prospective volunteer hopes to gain from the experience, not only why the cause matters to them. Recognise that most volunteers are motivated by more than one function at once, rather than assuming a single, uniform motivation across your whole volunteer base. Design roles and experiences with specific functions in mind, a role offering visible skill development serves the Understanding function, a role with strong team interaction serves the Social function. Revisit this understanding periodically, since a volunteer's motivation can shift over the course of their involvement.
Worked Example

Bosede coordinates a volunteer reading programme for children in Ondo, Nigeria, and had assumed, without really examining it, that every volunteer who signed up shared the same values-based motivation she herself felt strongly. Working through this session's framework during her next recruitment round, she began asking a simple, direct question in every intake conversation, what a prospective volunteer hoped to gain from the experience.

The answers surprised her. Several university students named the Career function explicitly, hoping the experience would strengthen applications for education-related work. One retired teacher named the Social function, missing the daily interaction her previous career had provided. Recognising this variety, Bosede adjusted her programme structure specifically, adding a written reference and a skills-completion certificate for volunteers motivated by career development, and building in more informal group time before and after sessions for volunteers seeking social connection, changes she credited directly with a noticeably stronger volunteer retention rate over her following recruitment cycle.
Common Pitfalls

A common mistake is assuming every volunteer shares the same values-based motivation the organiser themselves feels, missing the real variety research on this topic consistently finds. Another is designing a single, uniform volunteer experience for everyone, without adapting anything to the different functions likely present across a diverse volunteer base. A third is forcing a volunteer into a single motivational category, when most people are actually motivated by a combination of functions simultaneously.
Why This Framework Matters for Retention

Research using this framework has found that volunteers whose actual experience matches their underlying motivation report higher satisfaction and are more likely to continue volunteering over time, compared to volunteers whose experience does not serve their real motivation, even if the volunteer work itself is objectively similar. This is the practical payoff of taking motivation seriously at the recruitment and role-design stage, rather than treating it as an interesting but ultimately optional detail: it directly connects to the retention challenge covered later in this course.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

This session introduced the functional approach to volunteer motivation, naming six distinct functions, Values, Understanding, Social, Career, Protective, and Enhancement, that volunteering can serve, often several at once for the same person. Bosede's reading programme example showed how a simple, direct question during recruitment revealed a real variety of motivations her assumption of universal altruism had been missing, and how adapting her programme to that variety improved her retention. The session closed by connecting this framework directly to retention, the topic covered in depth later in this course.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a time you volunteered, or considered volunteering. Which of the six functions, Values, Understanding, Social, Career, Protective, Enhancement, best describes what you were actually hoping to get from it?

2. For a current or planned volunteer role in your own work, which function or functions do you suspect it currently serves best, and which does it currently serve poorly? Practical Output: Practical Output A short profile of two real or imagined volunteers for your programme, naming the likely motivational function or functions for each and one specific way your programme could serve that motivation.
References and Further Reading

•   Clary, E.G., Snyder, M., Ridge, R.D., Copeland, J., Stukas, A.A., Haugen, J., & Miene, P. (1998). Understanding and assessing the motivations of volunteers: A functional approach. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 74(6), 1516-1530.

lessons.title: Study Session 2: Recruiting the Right Volunteers

blocks.text: Study Session 2: Recruiting the Right Volunteers

This session builds practical recruitment skill, applying the motivation framework from the previous session to sourcing volunteers and writing role descriptions that actually speak to what a prospective volunteer is looking for.
Learning Outcomes

•   Identify appropriate recruitment channels for different types of volunteer roles. •   Write a role description that speaks to a specific motivational function rather than a generic appeal. •   Screen volunteers appropriately for the specific role being filled. •   Set realistic expectations during recruitment to prevent early volunteer dropout. •   Apply these recruitment practices to a real volunteer role in your own programme.
Main Content
Choosing the Right Recruitment Channel

Different recruitment channels tend to attract volunteers with different underlying motivations, and choosing a channel deliberately, rather than defaulting to whichever is easiest to use, improves the chances of attracting volunteers truly suited to a specific role. A university career centre or student organisation tends to attract volunteers with a strong Career function. A faith community or existing social network tends to attract volunteers with strong Values or Social functions. A corporate volunteering partnership often brings people whose motivation blends Career and Values functions.

A channel does not determine motivation perfectly, though understanding the general tendency helps target recruitment effort toward the channels most likely to produce volunteers well matched to a specific role's actual demands and rewards.
Writing a Role Description That Speaks to Motivation

A generic role description, focused only on tasks and time commitment, misses the opportunity to speak directly to what a prospective volunteer is actually looking for. A role description written with a specific motivational function in mind names both what the volunteer will do and what they stand to gain, skill development for the Understanding function, team collaboration for the Social function, a reference and demonstrable experience for the Career function.

This does not mean fabricating benefits a role does not actually offer. It means being deliberate and explicit about the real benefits a role does provide, rather than leaving a prospective volunteer to guess or discover them only after committing.
Screening Appropriately for the Role

Not every volunteer role requires the same level of screening, and matching screening rigour to the role's actual demands and risks, particularly where the role involves working directly with vulnerable groups such as children, protects both the organisation and the people it serves. A role involving direct, unsupervised contact with

children warrants formal background checks and reference verification. A role involving occasional, supervised event support at a public gathering typically does not require the same level of scrutiny.

Over-screening a low-risk role can discourage willing volunteers with an unnecessarily burdensome process, while under-screening a high-risk role creates real safety and reputational exposure. Matching the screening level honestly to the actual role protects against both failure modes.
Key Practices

Choose recruitment channels deliberately, matched to the motivational profile a specific role is best suited to attract. Write role descriptions that name the specific, real benefit a volunteer stands to gain, not only the tasks involved. Match screening rigour to the actual risk and responsibility level of the role, neither over-screening a low-risk role nor under-screening a high-risk one. Set realistic expectations about time commitment and actual role demands during recruitment itself, rather than allowing a mismatch to surface only after a volunteer has already started.
Worked Example

Thandi coordinates volunteer recruitment for a community health outreach programme in Bloemfontein, South Africa, and had been posting an identical, generic volunteer call across every channel available to her, resulting in a high early dropout rate among new volunteers within their first month. Reviewing this session's guidance, she recognised her generic posting attracted a wide mix of motivations without preparing any of them well for the specific role's actual demands, long walking distances between households, direct exposure to difficult health situations, and limited opportunity for the kind of social interaction some volunteers were implicitly expecting.

She rewrote her role description to name these realities explicitly alongside the actual benefits, structured clinical exposure valuable for volunteers with a Career function interested in health fields, and a specific note that the role suited someone comfortable working more independently than in a highly social team setting. Her next recruitment round attracted fewer total applicants but a noticeably lower first-month dropout rate, since volunteers arriving now had an accurate picture of what the role actually involved and had self-selected accordingly.
Common Pitfalls

A common mistake is posting an identical, generic volunteer call across every channel and role, missing the chance to target recruitment effort toward volunteers actually well suited to a specific role's demands, exactly the pattern Thandi's example corrected. Another is applying uniform screening rigour to every role regardless of actual risk, either discouraging willing volunteers for low-risk work or under-protecting a high-risk one. A third is describing a role attractively without naming its real demands, leading to early dropout once a volunteer's real experience does not match the expectations recruitment created.
Recruitment as the First Step in Retention

It helps to think of recruitment as the first and arguably most important step in retention, rather than a separate, earlier stage disconnected from it. A volunteer recruited with an accurate, motivation-matched picture of a role arrives already better positioned to stay engaged than one recruited through a generic, unfocused appeal, since the mismatch that so often drives early dropout was largely prevented before it could occur. The practices in this session are, in this sense, retention practices applied at the earliest possible point.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

This session built practical recruitment skill, covering how to choose recruitment channels matched to a role's likely motivational profile, write role descriptions naming specific, honest benefits rather than generic appeals, and screen volunteers proportionately to actual role risk. Thandi's community health example showed how naming a role's real demands honestly, alongside its actual benefits, produced fewer total applicants but a considerably lower early dropout rate than a generic recruitment call had achieved. The session closed by framing recruitment as the earliest stage of retention, since a well-matched volunteer starts already better positioned to stay engaged.
Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a volunteer role, real or imagined, in your own work. Which recruitment channel would likely attract volunteers truly well suited to it?

2. If you wrote a role description for that same role, what specific, real benefit would you name, beyond the tasks involved? Practical Output: Practical Output A role description for one real or planned volunteer role, naming its actual demands honestly alongside a specific, real benefit tied to a likely motivational function, plus a note on the recruitment channel you would use.
References and Further Reading

•   Clary, E.G., Snyder, M., Ridge, R.D., Copeland, J., Stukas, A.A., Haugen, J., & Miene, P. (1998). Understanding and assessing the motivations of volunteers: A functional approach. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 74(6), 1516-1530.

lessons.title: Study Session 3: Onboarding, Supervision, and Volunteer Experience

blocks.text: Study Session 3: Onboarding, Supervision, and Volunteer Experience

Research on volunteer programmes consistently identifies the earliest weeks as the point most volunteer programmes actually lose people. This session covers structured onboarding and clear ongoing supervision, the practices that determine whether a well-recruited volunteer actually stays.
Learning Outcomes

•   Explain why the onboarding period is disproportionately important for volunteer retention. •   Build a structured onboarding process appropriate for a small organisation. •   Provide role clarity that prevents common early volunteer confusion. •   Supervise volunteers in a way that supports rather than micromanages them. •   Apply these practices to your own programme's onboarding process.
Main Content
Why the Early Weeks Matter Disproportionately

A volunteer's first few weeks shape their entire impression of whether the role matches what recruitment promised, whether the organisation actually has its logistics together, and whether they feel truly useful or merely tolerated. A poor early experience, confusion about what to do, a disorganised first session, a sense of being unwelcome or unnecessary, can undo even the strongest recruitment match, since a volunteer who arrives well matched to a role can still leave quickly if the actual onboarding experience feels chaotic or unwelcoming.

This is why structured onboarding deserves deliberate investment disproportionate to its brief duration relative to a volunteer's total time with an organisation. A strong first few weeks builds the foundation everything else, including the recognition and retention practices covered later in this course, is built on.
Building a Structured Onboarding Process

A structured onboarding process for a small organisation can stay simple, while still consistently covering several elements: an orientation to the organisation's mission and the specific programme the volunteer is joining, clear role expectations, an introduction to key staff and fellow volunteers, and enough initial guided practice that the volunteer feels reasonably confident before being left to work independently.

Consistency matters as much as content. An onboarding process that varies significantly depending on who happens to be available to run it on a given day produces uneven experiences and, over time, an uneven sense among volunteers of whether the organisation is actually well run. A simple, written onboarding checklist, followed consistently regardless of who delivers it, protects against this drift.
Providing Role Clarity

Confusion about what is actually expected is one of the most common sources of early volunteer discomfort and dropout. Clear role clarity means a volunteer understands, from the very start, specifically what tasks they are responsible for, what decisions they are authorised to make independently versus what needs to be escalated, and who to actually go to with a question.

This clarity benefits from being written down, not only communicated verbally during a single orientation session a new volunteer may not fully absorb in the moment. A simple, one-page role summary a volunteer can refer back to protects against the specific kind of early confusion that a purely verbal explanation, however well delivered, can fail to fully retain.
Key Practices

Build a consistent, written onboarding checklist covering orientation, role expectations, introductions, and guided initial practice, followed the same way regardless of who delivers it. Provide a written role summary a volunteer can refer back to, not only a verbal explanation during orientation. Name specifically who a volunteer should go to with a question, rather than leaving this to be discovered informally. Check in specifically during the first few weeks, not only at the point of a formal problem, since this is the period most vulnerable to early, preventable dropout.
Worked Example

Nnenna coordinates a volunteer literacy programme in Orlu, Nigeria, and noticed a consistent pattern over several recruitment cycles, a meaningful share of new volunteers stopped showing up within their first three sessions, despite seeming truly enthusiastic during recruitment conversations. Reviewing her actual onboarding process, she realised it varied considerably depending on which staff member happened to be available on a new volunteer's first day, sometimes thorough, sometimes rushed, with no consistent written material a volunteer could refer back to afterward.

She built a simple, written onboarding checklist, along with a one-page role summary covering exactly what a literacy volunteer was responsible for and who to contact with questions, and required every staff member delivering onboarding to follow the same checklist regardless of how busy that particular day happened to be. She also added a specific, scheduled check-in after each new volunteer's second session, rather than waiting to hear from them only if a problem arose. Her early dropout rate dropped noticeably over her next several recruitment cycles, and she attributed the change specifically to consistency and the written role summary, rather than to any change in the volunteers she was actually recruiting.
Common Pitfalls

A common mistake is allowing onboarding quality to vary depending on who happens to deliver it, producing inconsistent early experiences that erode confidence in the organisation's overall reliability, exactly the pattern Nnenna's example corrected. Another is relying only on verbal explanation during a single orientation session, without written material a volunteer can refer back to once questions inevitably arise later. A third is waiting for a volunteer to raise a problem rather than proactively checking in during the specifically vulnerable early weeks.
Supervision That Supports Rather Than Micromanages

Once onboarding is complete, ongoing supervision works best when it strikes a balance between providing real support and respecting a volunteer's growing independence. Excessive, close oversight can feel to a volunteer like a lack of trust, particularly once they have demonstrated basic competence, while too little contact can leave a volunteer feeling unsupported and uncertain whether their work is actually valued or even noticed. Regular, brief, scheduled check-ins, rather than either constant oversight or near-total absence, tend to strike this balance well, giving a volunteer a reliable, predictable point of contact without hovering over their day-to- day work.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

This session covered why a volunteer's earliest weeks disproportionately shape retention, and built practical skill in structured, consistent onboarding and clear role clarity that protects against this vulnerable early period. Nnenna's literacy programme example showed how replacing an inconsistent, staff-dependent onboarding process with a written checklist and role summary, plus a proactive early check-in, noticeably reduced early dropout without any change to actual volunteer recruitment. The session closed by describing balanced, regular supervision, neither micromanaging nor absent, as the practice that sustains a volunteer's confidence and sense of being valued once onboarding is complete.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a time you started a new role, paid or volunteer, and the onboarding felt disorganised or rushed. How did that affect your early confidence and commitment?

2. For your own volunteer programme, does onboarding currently vary depending on who delivers it, or is it consistent regardless of staff availability? Practical Output: Practical Output A written onboarding checklist and a one-page role summary for one real volunteer role in your programme, plus a specific scheduled check-in point during the volunteer's first few weeks.
References and Further Reading
This session draws on general practitioner knowledge and the frameworks introduced earlier in this course; no new citation is introduced here.

blocks.text: Study Session 4: Recognition and Retention

This session closes the volunteer-focused half of this course by covering recognition tailored to what actually motivates a specific volunteer, and practical strategies for preventing the kind of burnout that quietly erodes even a well-onboarded volunteer's commitment over time.
Learning Outcomes

•   Explain why generic recognition can fail to actually motivate a specific volunteer. •   Design recognition practices matched to different motivational functions. •   Identify early warning signs of volunteer burnout before they lead to dropout. •   Build sustainable volunteering practices that protect against burnout structurally. •   Apply these recognition and retention practices to your own volunteer programme.
Main Content
Why Generic Recognition Falls Short

A standard certificate of appreciation or a public thank-you at an event is a reasonable default, but it does not equally serve every volunteer's underlying motivation. A volunteer motivated primarily by the Career function benefits far more from a specific, detailed written reference documenting concrete skills and achievements than from a generic certificate. A volunteer motivated by the Social function may value public acknowledgement among the team considerably more than a volunteer motivated primarily by Values, who might find quiet, private thanks more meaningful than public recognition.

This connects directly back to the motivation framework introduced earlier in this course. Recognition, to actually motivate rather than merely satisfy an organisational obligation to say thank you, benefits from being tailored to what a specific volunteer is actually looking for, in the same way a well-designed role is.
Matching Recognition to Motivation

For the Understanding function, recognition might take the form of additional training opportunities or visible acknowledgement of new skills gained. For the Career function, a specific written reference, a LinkedIn recommendation, or an introduction to a relevant professional contact serves the underlying motivation directly. For the Social function, public acknowledgement, team celebrations, or simply more informal time together serves the motivation well. For the Values function, connecting a volunteer directly to the tangible impact of their work, a specific story or outcome their effort contributed to, often resonates more than a generic thank-you.

This does not require an elaborate, individualised recognition system for every volunteer. Even a simple practice of asking, during onboarding, what kind of recognition would actually feel meaningful to a specific volunteer builds this matching into a programme without significant added complexity.
Recognising Early Warning Signs of Burnout

Volunteer burnout often shows warning signs before it results in outright dropout: declining energy or enthusiasm noticeable during sessions, increasingly frequent cancellations or lateness, a shift from proactive

engagement to going through the motions, or explicit comments about feeling overwhelmed or stretched thin. Noticing these signs early, rather than only after a volunteer has already stopped showing up, creates a window for a supportive conversation and, where appropriate, an adjustment to workload or role before the situation reaches a breaking point.

A regular, brief check-in habit, distinct from a formal performance review, makes noticing these early signs considerably more likely, since it creates a natural, low-pressure opportunity for a volunteer to mention feeling stretched before it becomes a crisis.
Key Practices

Ask volunteers directly, ideally during onboarding, what kind of recognition would actually feel meaningful to them. Match recognition practices to the motivational functions relevant to your specific volunteer base, rather than relying on one generic approach for everyone. Build regular, brief check-ins into your programme specifically to catch early signs of burnout before they lead to dropout. Adjust workload or role proactively when a volunteer shows early signs of strain, rather than waiting until they raise a formal complaint or simply stop showing up.
Worked Example

Furaha coordinates a volunteer environmental cleanup programme in Dodoma, Tanzania, and had relied entirely on a standard end-of-year certificate ceremony as her programme's only recognition practice, a single annual event that felt increasingly disconnected from the actual, ongoing work volunteers did throughout the year. Applying this session's guidance, she began asking new volunteers directly during onboarding what kind of recognition would actually feel meaningful to them, and found the answers varied considerably, some wanted a written reference for job applications, others simply wanted their specific contribution mentioned by name during team updates.

She built a lightweight system tracking each volunteer's stated recognition preference, and began delivering smaller, more frequent, individually matched recognition throughout the year rather than relying solely on the single annual ceremony. She also noticed, through a newly instituted monthly check-in, that one of her longest- serving volunteers had begun showing early signs of burnout, increasing lateness and visibly lower energy, and was able to have a supportive conversation and adjust that volunteer's workload before the volunteer reached the point of quitting entirely, something she believed would likely have happened without the regular check-in habit catching the signs early.
Common Pitfalls

A common mistake is relying on a single, generic recognition practice for an entire volunteer base, missing the chance to actually motivate volunteers through recognition matched to what they specifically value, exactly the gap Furaha's example closed. Another is waiting for a volunteer to explicitly raise a burnout concern before responding, rather than proactively watching for early warning signs through regular check-ins. A third is treating recognition as a single annual event rather than an ongoing practice woven throughout a volunteer's time with an organisation.
Building Sustainability Into the Programme Itself

Beyond individual recognition and burnout awareness, sustainable volunteering benefits from structural protections built into the programme's design itself: realistic workload expectations set clearly during

recruitment, built-in flexibility for volunteers to take breaks without guilt or penalty, and a culture that treats a volunteer stepping back temporarily as a normal, accepted part of sustainable involvement rather than a failure or a letdown. A programme that structurally protects against overload, rather than relying entirely on individual volunteers to self-manage their own limits, tends to retain people over a considerably longer period.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

This session covered why generic recognition often fails to actually motivate, tying recognition practices back to the motivational framework introduced earlier in this course, and covered recognising early warning signs of burnout before they lead to dropout. Furaha's environmental cleanup example showed how asking volunteers directly what recognition would feel meaningful to them, combined with a regular check-in habit, let her both deliver more effective recognition and catch a case of early burnout before a long-serving volunteer reached the point of quitting. The session closed by framing sustainable volunteering as something a programme should build structurally into its own design, not something left entirely to individual volunteers to self-manage.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a time you received recognition, at work, as a volunteer, or elsewhere, that felt truly meaningful versus one that felt generic or obligatory. What was the actual difference?

2. If you checked in with your own volunteers regularly, what early warning sign of burnout do you suspect you might currently be missing? Practical Output: Practical Output A recognition plan for your volunteer base, matching at least three different recognition approaches to three different motivational functions, plus a specific check-in schedule for catching early burnout signs.
References and Further Reading

•   Clary, E.G., Snyder, M., Ridge, R.D., Copeland, J., Stukas, A.A., Haugen, J., & Miene, P. (1998). Understanding and assessing the motivations of volunteers: A functional approach. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 74(6), 1516-1530.

lessons.title: Study Session 5: Mapping and Prioritising Stakeholders

blocks.text: Study Session 5: Mapping and Prioritising Stakeholders

This session shifts from volunteers specifically to the broader set of stakeholders any social-impact effort depends on, introducing a widely used tool for mapping who actually needs close, ongoing management and who needs only lighter, less resource-intensive engagement.
Learning Outcomes

•   Define a stakeholder in the context of social-impact work. •   Explain the power-interest matrix and its two dimensions. •   Place a real stakeholder accurately within the matrix's four quadrants. •   Match an appropriate engagement strategy to each quadrant. •   Apply this mapping process to your own programme's stakeholders.
Main Content
Who Counts as a Stakeholder

A stakeholder is any individual or group who can affect, or is affected by, a programme's work, a category considerably broader than the beneficiaries a programme directly serves. Government regulators, community leaders, funders, partner organisations, volunteers, staff, and the beneficiaries themselves are all stakeholders, though each holds a different kind and degree of influence over, and interest in, the programme's actual work.

Trying to engage every stakeholder with equal intensity is neither realistic nor an efficient use of a small organisation's limited time and resources. This is exactly the problem a structured mapping tool is built to solve, by helping an organisation decide deliberately where its limited engagement effort should actually go.
The Power-Interest Matrix

A widely used stakeholder mapping tool plots stakeholders along two dimensions: power, a stakeholder's ability to influence the programme's strategy, resources, or continued operation, and interest, how much a stakeholder actually cares about, or is affected by, the programme's outcome. Plotting stakeholders across these two dimensions produces four quadrants, each calling for a distinctly different engagement approach.

High power, high interest stakeholders, a major funder, for instance, need close, active management, since they both care deeply about outcomes and hold real ability to affect the programme's future. High power, low interest stakeholders, a government regulator holding real authority over the programme despite not being specifically focused on it, need to be kept satisfied through periodic, appropriate engagement, without demanding the same intensive relationship-building a high-interest stakeholder requires. Low power, high interest stakeholders, often including the community directly served by a programme, need to be kept truly informed and engaged, since their interest is real even though their formal power over programme decisions may be limited. Low power, low interest stakeholders need only light, minimal monitoring, without significant investment of limited engagement resources.
Placing Stakeholders Accurately

Placing a stakeholder accurately within the matrix requires honest assessment, resisting the temptation to place every stakeholder in the high power, high interest quadrant simply because engaging everyone intensively feels safer or more respectful. A stakeholder's actual position can also shift over time, a government agency with low interest in a small pilot programme might move to high interest once that programme demonstrates results worth scaling, and a mapping exercise conducted once at a programme's start should be periodically revisited rather than treated as permanently fixed.

It also helps to remember that power and interest are somewhat independent of each other. A stakeholder can hold considerable formal power while actually caring very little about a specific programme's outcome, and a stakeholder with very little formal power, a community member directly affected by a programme's work, can still care deeply and hold valuable, ground-level insight the programme truly needs.
Key Practices

List every group or individual who can affect, or is affected by, your programme's work before beginning to prioritise, so no relevant stakeholder is missed from the outset. Assess power and interest honestly and independently for each stakeholder, resisting the temptation to place everyone in the high-priority quadrant by default. Revisit the mapping periodically, since a stakeholder's actual position can shift meaningfully as a programme develops. Match engagement intensity and approach to each stakeholder's actual quadrant, rather than applying a uniform level of engagement effort across every stakeholder regardless of position.
Worked Example

Khadija runs a small maternal health advocacy initiative in Gombe, Nigeria, and had been spending roughly equal time and effort engaging every stakeholder connected to her work, from her primary funder to a local government health office to individual community members, without any deliberate sense of where her limited time was actually best spent. Working through the power-interest matrix honestly for the first time, she placed her primary funder in the high power, high interest quadrant, confirming the intensive relationship-building effort she had already been investing there was well justified.

More usefully, she recognised she had been under-investing in the local government health office, a stakeholder she had initially assumed had low interest in her small-scale programme and had therefore engaged only minimally, when in fact the office held considerable formal power over facility access her programme actually depended on. Reclassifying this stakeholder into the high power, low interest quadrant, she built a more deliberate, periodic engagement plan specifically aimed at keeping this office satisfied and informed, a shift she credited with resolving a facility access delay that had been quietly slowing her programme for months.
Common Pitfalls

A common mistake is spreading engagement effort roughly equally across every stakeholder without deliberate prioritisation, exactly the pattern Khadija's example moved past once she mapped her stakeholders honestly. Another is underestimating a stakeholder's actual power because their interest currently appears low, missing a real risk or opportunity that stakeholder's actual influence represents. A third is mapping stakeholders once at a programme's start and never revisiting the exercise as circumstances and stakeholder positions actually change.
Beyond the Matrix: A Starting Point, Not a Final Answer

The power-interest matrix is a useful starting structure rather than a complete or final answer to stakeholder management on its own. It tells an organisation roughly where to direct engagement effort, while the actual content and quality of that engagement, covered in the closing session of this course, still requires real relationship-building skill the matrix itself does not provide. Treating the matrix as a planning tool that informs deliberate strategy, rather than a mechanical formula that replaces real judgement, keeps its use truly useful rather than reductive.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

This session introduced the power-interest matrix, a stakeholder mapping tool plotting power, a stakeholder's ability to influence a programme, against interest, how much they actually care about its outcome, producing four quadrants each calling for a different engagement approach. Khadija's maternal health example showed how mapping her stakeholders honestly revealed she had been under-investing in a high-power, low-interest local government office, a reclassification that led to a more deliberate engagement plan resolving a facility access issue that had quietly stalled her programme. The session closed by framing the matrix as a useful starting structure for deliberate strategy, not a replacement for the real relationship-building skill covered in the closing session.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. List three stakeholders connected to your own programme. Where would you honestly place each one on the power-interest matrix, before reading further in this course?

2. Is there a stakeholder you suspect you might be under-investing in, similar to Khadija's local government office, because their interest currently appears lower than their actual power? Practical Output: Practical Output A power-interest matrix for at least five real stakeholders connected to your programme, with each placed in a specific quadrant and a brief note on why.
References and Further Reading
•   Mendelow, A.L. (1991). Environmental scanning: The impact of the stakeholder concept. Proceedings from the Second International Conference on Information Systems, 407-418. Cambridge, MA.

lessons.title: Study Session 6: Building Ongoing Stakeholder Relationships

blocks.text: Study Session 6: Building Ongoing Stakeholder Relationships

This closing session moves from mapping stakeholders to actually engaging them well over time, matching engagement strategies to each matrix quadrant and closing out both this course and the volunteer and stakeholder work it has built.
Learning Outcomes

•   Design an engagement strategy specifically matched to each power-interest quadrant. •   Communicate effectively with stakeholders holding different levels of power and interest. •   Sustain stakeholder relationships over a programme's full life, not only at its start. •   Recognise when a stakeholder relationship needs course correction. •   Apply a complete stakeholder engagement plan to your own programme.
Main Content
Engagement Strategies for Each Quadrant

High power, high interest stakeholders warrant real, ongoing partnership: regular, substantive communication, involvement in real decisions where appropriate, and responsiveness to their concerns and questions. High power, low interest stakeholders warrant a lighter but still deliberate touch, periodic updates that keep them satisfied and informed without demanding significant time from either side, since over-engaging a stakeholder with truly low interest can feel intrusive rather than respectful.

Low power, high interest stakeholders, often a programme's own beneficiary community, warrant consistent, accessible information and real channels for feedback, since their formal power may be limited but their stake in outcomes is real and their insight often valuable. Low power, low interest stakeholders warrant only light, occasional monitoring, checking periodically whether their position has shifted, without investing significant ongoing engagement effort that would be better directed elsewhere.
Communicating Across Different Stakeholder Types

Communication that works well for one stakeholder type often does not translate directly to another. A funder in the high power, high interest quadrant typically expects formal, data-driven communication, aligned with the reporting practices covered earlier in this pathway. A beneficiary community in the low power, high interest quadrant typically responds better to accessible, conversational communication in a familiar format, closer to the community-facing reporting approach also covered earlier in this pathway.

The underlying information should remain consistent and truthful across all stakeholders, with the format, technical depth, and channel adapting to who is actually receiving it, rather than communicating less honestly or substantively with any one group, in the same way tailoring a proposal's framing to different funder types, covered earlier in this pathway, did not change the proposal's underlying substance.
Sustaining Relationships Over a Programme's Full Life

Stakeholder engagement often receives the most attention at a programme's launch, when relationships are actively being built, and then quietly fades as day-to-day delivery work takes over. Sustaining engagement
across a programme's full life, beyond only its start, protects against relationships that were carefully built early on and then allowed to weaken through simple neglect over time.

A useful practice is scheduling stakeholder engagement activities on the same kind of regular calendar used for M&E review, covered earlier in this pathway, rather than leaving engagement to happen only when a specific need arises. This turns relationship maintenance from an occasional, reactive activity into a consistent, planned part of a programme's ongoing operation.
Key Practices

Design a specific engagement approach for each of the four power-interest quadrants, rather than a single, uniform strategy applied to every stakeholder. Adapt communication format and depth to each stakeholder type while keeping the underlying information consistent and honest across all of them. Schedule stakeholder engagement activities regularly across a programme's full life, not only intensively at its launch. Watch for signs a stakeholder relationship needs course correction, declining responsiveness, a shift in a stakeholder's actual position on the matrix, or growing tension, and address these signs proactively rather than only once they become a serious problem.
Worked Example

Lerato runs a small youth empowerment initiative in Francistown, Botswana, and had invested heavily in stakeholder relationships during her programme's initial launch, personal visits, detailed presentations, careful relationship-building with her funder, local government contacts, and community leaders, but found this intensity naturally faded as she became consumed by day-to-day programme delivery over the following year. She noticed, roughly a year in, that her relationship with a key local government contact felt noticeably weaker than it had at launch, without any specific incident she could point to, simply gradual neglect.

Applying this session's guidance, she built stakeholder engagement directly into her existing quarterly M&E review calendar, scheduling a specific, brief check-in with each of her high-power stakeholders at the same time she reviewed her programme data, rather than treating engagement as a separate activity competing for attention she often did not have. This structural change meant her key relationships received consistent, if modest, ongoing attention throughout the year rather than only intensive attention at launch followed by drift, and she noted her local government relationship recovered noticeably once this consistent contact resumed.
Common Pitfalls

A common mistake is investing heavily in stakeholder relationships at a programme's launch and then allowing that engagement to fade through simple neglect as delivery work takes over, exactly the pattern Lerato's example corrected. Another is communicating with every stakeholder in the same format and technical depth, regardless of what actually suits their specific type and needs. A third is failing to notice early signs that a relationship needs attention, addressing tension or drift only once it has become a serious, harder-to-resolve problem.
Bringing Volunteers and Stakeholders Together

Across this course, volunteers and broader stakeholders have been treated somewhat separately, but it is worth closing by recognising that volunteers are themselves a specific kind of stakeholder, often falling into the high interest, variable power quadrant depending on their role and level of involvement, and the same underlying discipline, understanding what someone actually needs and wants, engaging them deliberately rather than

generically, and sustaining that engagement over time rather than only at the start, runs through both halves of this course. A social-impact effort that treats both its volunteers and its broader stakeholders with this same deliberate, sustained attention builds the kind of durable, trusted relationships that carry a programme well beyond what any single skilled individual could accomplish alone.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

This closing session matched specific engagement strategies to each power-interest quadrant, covered adapting communication format and depth to different stakeholder types while keeping underlying information consistent, and emphasised sustaining engagement across a programme's full life rather than only at its launch. Lerato's youth empowerment example showed how building stakeholder check-ins directly into an existing quarterly review calendar, rather than treating engagement as a separate competing activity, restored a government relationship that had weakened through simple neglect over her programme's first year. The course closed by recognising volunteers as a specific kind of stakeholder, and naming the shared discipline, deliberate, motivation-aware, sustained engagement, that runs through both the volunteer and broader stakeholder halves of this course.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a relationship, professional or otherwise, that felt strong at the start but weakened over time through simple neglect rather than any specific conflict. What might have sustained it?

2. Across this entire course, volunteer motivation, recruitment, onboarding, recognition, and stakeholder mapping and engagement, which single practice do you think would make the biggest difference in your own work if you started it this month? Practical Output: Practical Output A complete stakeholder engagement plan naming a specific strategy for each power-interest quadrant from the previous session, plus a schedule for sustaining engagement across your programme's full life, not only at its launch.
References and Further Reading
This session draws on general practitioner knowledge and the frameworks introduced earlier in this course; no new citation is introduced here.

quiz.q: According to this session, why might a standard certificate of appreciation fail to actually motivate every volunteer?
options: Certificates are never appropriate for volunteers
Recognition has no real effect on volunteer retention
Different volunteers are motivated by different functions, and a generic form of recognition does not equally serve all of them
Only paid staff respond to any form of recognition
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Recognition and Retention) before continuing.

quiz.q: What kind of recognition does this session suggest for a volunteer motivated primarily by the Career function?
options: A generic thank-you card only
No recognition is necessary for this function
Public acknowledgement at a large event only
A specific, detailed written reference documenting concrete skills and achievements
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Recognition and Retention) before continuing.

quiz.q: In Furaha's example, what did her regular check-in habit allow her to catch?
options: Early signs of burnout in a long-serving volunteer, allowing a supportive conversation before they quit

A recruitment channel problem
An onboarding inconsistency
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Recognition and Retention) before continuing.

quiz.q: What are the two dimensions of the power-interest matrix?
options: Power, the ability to influence a programme, and interest, how much a stakeholder cares about its outcome
Cost and benefit
Time and money
Risk and reward
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Mapping and Prioritising Stakeholders) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to this session, how should a high power, low interest stakeholder generally be engaged?
options: Ignored entirely
Kept satisfied through periodic, appropriate engagement, without the same intensity as a high-interest stakeholder
Engaged with the exact same intensity as a major funder
Removed from the stakeholder list
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Mapping and Prioritising Stakeholders) before continuing.

quiz.q: In Khadija's example, what stakeholder had she been under-investing in, and why?
options: Her primary funder, because she assumed they had low power

A partner organisation with no real influence
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Mapping and Prioritising Stakeholders) before continuing.

options: Volunteers never actually differ from one another
Research consistently finds volunteers are motivated by several distinct, differing functions, not one uniform reason
Motivation does not matter for volunteer programmes
Only paid staff have real motivations

options: Values
Social
Career
Protective

She added a written reference and a skills-completion certificate
She required a formal application fee
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Why People Volunteer) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: According to this session, why does choosing a recruitment channel deliberately matter?
options: Different channels tend to attract volunteers with different underlying motivations, so choosing deliberately improves matching to a role
Recruitment channel has no real effect on outcomes
All channels attract identical volunteers
Only paid advertising channels are effective

options: Nothing else is necessary
Only the organisation's mission statement
The names of other volunteers
The specific, real benefit a volunteer stands to gain from the role

options: Naming the role's real demands honestly alongside its actual benefits, allowing better self-selection
Increasing the number of volunteers recruited
Removing all screening requirements
Shortening the volunteer commitment period
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Recruiting the Right Volunteers) before continuing.

options: It has no real effect on retention
A poor early experience can undo even a strong recruitment match, since it shapes a volunteer's entire impression of the organisation
Onboarding is the only stage that affects retention at all

A consistent, written onboarding checklist followed the same way regardless of who delivers it

Only onboarding volunteers once a year in a single large batch

options: Reducing the number of volunteers recruited
Removing all volunteer supervision entirely
A written onboarding checklist, a role summary, and a proactive early check-in after the second session
Extending the required volunteer commitment period
